newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr resigned to range this side of July.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr resigned to range this side of July.

text.p: The Australian dollar barely budged through a muted session Monday and all the signs were it would not be moving anywhere this side of July.
A dearth of domestic data meant the loudest sound in dealing rooms was the complaints of how quiet it was.

"Put it this way; volatility is well offered and offers of lunch well bid," said one wag. "US$0.7450/7550 looks solidly established and people here are content to leave it that way until we see which way the RBA jumps next week."
The Reserve Bank holds its monthly board meeting on July 1 and the market supects an official rate cut will be the result.

By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was reclining at US$0.7510/15 having not stirred from a US$0.7502/7514 range all day. It had made it as high as US$0.7541 offshore Friday from US$0.7511/16 late here, but ran into sizeable sell orders before it could tackle important chart resistance at US$0.7550.
A break beyond there was the minimum needed to counter the present bearish mood and the currency would have to clear US$0.7630/7680 to reverse the trend completely.
Support was put at US$0.7490, US$0.7470 and US$0.7450 with a breach of the latter seen as confirmation of a new phase of the three-month-old five-cent-wide downtrend toward 73 cents.
On the crosses the local dollar tracked a firmer US$/yen up to 86.63/73 yen from 85.90/00 late Friday and crept ahead to 57.2 in trade weighted terms from 57.1.
Traders said both dollars benefited from a lack of official comment on currencies at the meeting of G7 leaders in Denver over the weekend.

The final statement merely rubber stamped previous pledges to cooperate for stable exchange rates, although President Bill Clinton did warn of trouble ahead if Japan's trade surplus exploded. The market did not seem too bothered itself and the US$ ended at 115.33/43 yen from 114.80/90 in New York Friday.
This was cold comfort for A$ bulls who have watched a remorseless decline from 80 cents in mid-March as the currency's historic interest rate advantage was snuffed out.
Domestic money rates here had moved well below those in the U.S. as the market priced in a fifth cut and at least one more tightening in the U.S., making it expensive to hold the A$.
Those still bullish longer term have clung to the hope that commodity prices would come to the rescue.
Above trend growth in the U.S. and recoveries in Japan and Europe, they argued, would lead to a synchronised world pickup and so to higher demand for, and prices of, commodities.

Such a rise would be a boon for Australia where commodities like coal and copper make up over 60 percent of exports. Many offshore investors also view the A$ as a surrogate for commodity trends and it has a good historical with prices in the past.

Base metals have shown improvement led by copper which recouped all the huge losses suffered in last year's Sumitomo scandal. This in turn helped the RBA's index of commodity prices rise 3.6 points so far this year to 94.2.
But many offshore funds tend to use the Commodity Research Bureau index of futures contracts which includes such un-Australian commodities as coffee, cocoa and orange juice.
The CRB has been much more erratic this year, starting around 240.00 it rose to nearly 255.00 in late May only to tumble back to 240.52 by the end of last week.
Some of the recent volatility was due to wild swings in coffee prices, but the underlying performance of the index hardly suggested the price boom A$ bulls were hoping for.

Without that the A$ would remain dominated by differentials and the outlook was not bright there with some analysts thinking the U.S. will have to hike two or three times. The process may start as soon as next week when the Federal Reserve holds its monthly policy meeting. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
